extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and practitioners seeking an encyclopedic overview of television (history, technology, standards, and formats)
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopaedic summary of television as a medium, covering its definition, history, technical evolution (mechanical, electronic, color, digital), transmission/distribution methods, display technologies, formats, and broadcast-related standards and artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of television as a medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Television (TV) is a telecommunication medium for transmitting moving images and sound; the term can also refer to a physical television set rather than the medium of transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a mass medium for advertising, entertainment, news, and sports; distinguishes television (audio+video) from radio (audio only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission media for television signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Television signals have been distributed as terrestrial broadcasts, by coaxial cable or optical fiber, via satellite systems, and, since the 2000s, via the Internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of distribution medium affects reach, infrastructure, and regulatory environment; historically terrestrial was dominant, while Internet streaming and cable/satellite grew later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analog versus digital signalling
rubrics_metrics.description: Until the early 2000s television signals were typically analog; a global transition to digital television (DTV) has been expected/undertaken, with digital transmissions multiplexed and compressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital TV enables multiple programs on the same channel bandwidth via compression; the transition changed standards, equipment and spectrum usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution and line standards (historical and modern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards mentioned include mechanical-era line counts and later standards such as 405-line, 525-line (US), 625-line (Soviet/Europe), as well as HDTV formats (720p, 1080i, 1080p) and progressive/interlaced variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Line/frame standards determine picture detail and compatibility; e.g., 525-line (NTSC) and 625-line (PAL/SECAM) were regionally adopted; HDTV offers substantially higher resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame rates and interlacing (progressive vs interlaced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast frame rates historically include 30 or 60 frames per second regions and interlaced formats (e.g., 576i, 480i); progressive formats (e.g., 720p, 1080p) transmit full frames each refresh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interlaced formats transmit alternate fields and were common for bandwidth reasons; progressive scanning is often preferred for motion clarity in modern systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color television systems (NTSC, PAL, SECAM and compatibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different color systems (NTSC, PAL, SECAM) were developed; NTSC/other systems encoded color information separately from brightness to conserve bandwidth and to be backwards compatible with black-and-white sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compatibility strategies allowed color transmissions to be received as black-and-white by older sets; color encoding choices impacted bandwidth and international compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bandwidth conservation and colour encoding
rubrics_metrics.description: One challenge was conserving radio spectrum when adding color — e.g., the US NTSC system encoded color information separately and reduced color resolution to save bandwidth while remaining compatible with monochrome sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design decisions (separate chroma encoding, reduced chroma resolution) were trade-offs between color fidelity and spectrum efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital television advantages (multiplexing, compression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of data compression, digital television can support more than one program on the same channel bandwidth and represents a major evolution in broadcasting capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital processing and inexpensive computing enabled DTV; compression standards and multiplexing determine channel capacity and services offered (e.g., multiple subchannels, EPG).

rubrics_metrics.name: Video formats and codec standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The article lists numerous video formats and standards and associated codecs, including MPEG-2, MPEG-4 Visual, MPEG-4 AVC, AVS, AVS2, MPEG-H HEVC, ATSC A/72, and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of codec/format affects compression efficiency, required bandwidth, device compatibility, and image quality; region and service (broadcast, satellite, streaming) influence which codecs are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audio standards used with television
rubrics_metrics.description: Audio codecs and standards referenced include AC-3 (5.1), AC-4, DTS, DRA, MPEG-1 Audio Layer II, MPEG Multichannel, PCM, LPCM, AAC, HE-AAC, and MPEG-H 3D Audio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audio format selection affects channel configurations (mono, stereo, 5.1), compatibility, and perceived quality; modern services may use advanced immersive audio standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden signals and ancillary data (VBI, teletext, closed captioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasts can carry hidden signals and ancillary data such as captioning, teletext, vertical blanking interval (VBI) services, AFD, EPG, and on-screen metadata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancillary channels are used for accessibility (closed captions), program guides, technical signalling and copy-control metadata; they are part of broadcast system design and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captioning and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Captioning is listed among audio/hidden signals and is an integral broadcast feature for accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provision of captions/subtitles is a content/accessibility expectation and in many jurisdictions a regulatory requirement for broadcast services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test cards and calibration (test patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard test items include television test cards and color bars such as SMPTE color bars, EBU colour bars, Indian-head test pattern, BBC Test Card and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test patterns are used when no program material is available and for calibration, alignment and troubleshooting of transmission and display equipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast-safe (content/technical constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'broadcast-safe' appears under technical issues, indicating constraints to ensure content is suitable for broadcast and conforms to technical/display limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensuring content is broadcast-safe can cover audio/video levels, legal/decency standards, closed-captioning, and technical formatting so that downstream transmission and receivers handle the signal reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards conversion and reverse standards conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards conversion processes are used to convert video between disparate broadcast standards (e.g., PAL↔NTSC) and may introduce artifacts; reverse standards conversion is also mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversion between line/frame/rate systems requires careful resampling; conversion quality impacts program portability across regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission system standards (System M, B/G, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article lists many analog and digital broadcasting system identifiers (e.g., System M for 525 lines, System B/C/G/H/I/K/L/N for 625/other lines) and associated color systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional broadcast systems define electrical/formatting specifications that manufacturers and broadcasters must follow for compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display technologies and hardware evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Display technologies discussed include CRT, fluorescent-backlit LCD, LED, OLED, plasma, DLP and the historical replacement of CRTs by flat-panel screens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display technology affects energy consumption, picture quality, size, form factor and market adoption; manufacturers' discontinuation of older technologies shapes available consumer options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smart TV and Internet television (streaming integration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Smart TVs with integrated Internet and Web 2.0 functions became dominant in the late 2010s, increasing availability of programs via streaming services (Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, iPlayer, Hulu).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration of Internet capability changes distribution models, user interaction, app ecosystems and platform-level considerations for content providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archival and consumer storage media for television content
rubrics_metrics.description: Various storage media enabled home viewing and archiving: Betamax, VHS, LaserDisc, HD hard drives, Video CDs, DVDs, flash drives, Blu-ray, DVRs and cloud video-on-demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Storage medium influences accessibility, quality retention, physical format constraints and how audiences time-shift viewing (e.g., recording vs streaming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-program support per channel (multiplexing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital television's use of multiplexed and compressed signals allows more than one program on the same channel bandwidth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplexing decisions determine channel lineups, bitrate per program and trade-offs between number of subchannels and per-program quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphics and on-screen presentation elements
rubrics_metrics.description: On-screen graphics referenced include lower thirds, digital on-screen graphics, news ticker, on-screen display, and score bugs used in broadcast design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphics design affects viewer comprehension and branding; placement and legibility need to be managed to avoid obscuring important image content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden/legacy signaling and content-control signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Signals such as the broadcast flag, CGMS-A, and other hidden signals are mentioned as mechanisms related to content control and metadata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These signals can carry copy-protection or rights-management metadata that devices and services may be required to respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical mechanical vs electronic television distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical television used Nipkow disks and low line counts (e.g., 30–120 lines); electronic television (camera tubes and CRTs) enabled higher resolution and practicality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding historical techniques clarifies the constraints that shaped early systems and why electronic/charge-storage designs displaced mechanical scanning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for high-definition and ultra-high-definition television
rubrics_metrics.description: HDTV standards (720p, 1080i, 1080p) and later UHDTV (4K, 8K) are referenced as providing substantially higher resolution compared to SDTV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption of HD/UHD involves transmission, codec, display and production workflow upgrades; format choice affects bandwidth and production complexity.
